1 Samuel opens in the last chaotic years of the judges. The tabernacle stands at Shiloh, but its priests, Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas, are corrupt, taking the best of the sacrifices and sleeping with the women who serve at the entrance (1 Sam 2:12-17; 1 Sam 2:22). The greatest threat is the Philistines, a people from the Aegean world who settled on the coast around 1175 BC. They had organised city-states, chariots, iron weapons and a monopoly on metalworking (1 Sam 13:19-22). Israel, a loose tribal league, could not match them.

When Israel takes the ark into battle like a lucky charm, the Philistines capture it and destroy Shiloh's power (1 Sam 4). Eli's daughter-in-law names her son Ichabod, 'where is the glory?', for 'the glory is departed from Israel' (1 Sam 4:21). But the ark humiliates the Philistine god Dagon and brings plague, until the Philistines send it back (1 Sam 5-6). The message: Israel's God cannot be controlled, and he fights his own battles.

The demand for a king (1 Sam 8) comes from real pressures: Samuel's sons are corrupt, and the Philistine threat needs a permanent army. But the people want a king 'like all the nations' (1 Sam 8:5, 1 Sam 8:20). God tells Samuel 'they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them' (1 Sam 8:7), yet he grants the request and chooses Saul. Scholars have long noted that the book contains both pro-monarchy and anti-monarchy strands (compare 1 Sam 9:15-17 with 1 Sam 8:10-18). The resolution is that kingship is acceptable if the king and people obey the LORD (1 Sam 12:13-15).

Saul starts well but fails when he offers sacrifice without waiting for Samuel (1 Sam 13:8-14) and keeps the spoils of Amalek (1 Sam 15). Samuel's verdict, 'to obey is better than sacrifice' (1 Sam 15:22), becomes a key prophetic theme. God sends Samuel to anoint David, the youngest son of Jesse in Bethlehem, because 'the LORD looketh on the heart' (1 Sam 16:7). The rest of the book traces the rise of David and the slow, tragic decline of Saul, who hunts David in jealousy while David refuses to harm 'the LORD's anointed' (1 Sam 24:6; 1 Sam 26:9). Many scholars read these chapters as an 'apology' defending David against the charge that he usurped Saul's throne.

39859:
In the Hebrew Bible, 1 and 2 Samuel form a single book among the Former Prophets. Its opening has a special place in Jewish worship: the story of Hannah and her prayer (1 Sam 1:1-2:10) is the haftarah read on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, because tradition says God 'remembered' Sarah, Rachel and Hannah on that day. The Talmud (Berakhot 31a) learns the laws of prayer from Hannah: she spoke in her heart, only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard (1 Sam 1:13). That is why the central Jewish prayer, the Amidah, is said quietly, with moving lips. Hannah's song, celebrating a God who brings down the mighty and lifts the poor (1 Sam 2:1-10), is one of the great theological poems of the Bible.

Samuel himself is honoured as a prophet equal to Moses and Aaron (Ps 99:6; Jer 15:1). He is the last judge and the first of the great prophets who anointed kings and confronted them. Jewish tradition is honest about Saul: the rabbis note that Saul was tall and humble at first (1 Sam 9:21; 1 Sam 10:22), and some say he lost the kingdom for one sin while David kept it despite many, because David repented sincerely while Saul made excuses (Yoma 22b discusses this contrast).

The first audience would hear 1 Samuel as a story about who truly rules Israel. Kings may be anointed, but the LORD remains Israel's King. The covenant relationship is not cancelled by the monarchy; the king must listen to God's word through the prophet. Hannah's song sets the tone: 'The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up' (1 Sam 2:7). The proud priests fall, the barren woman sings, the tall king fails and the youngest shepherd is chosen.

After Saul's death, David moves cautiously. He mourns Saul and Jonathan in a moving lament (2 Sam 1:17-27), is anointed king over Judah at Hebron, and waits seven years while Saul's son Ish-bosheth rules the northern tribes. Only after a long civil war and the murders of Abner and Ish-bosheth (which David condemns) do the northern tribes come to Hebron and make a covenant with him (2 Sam 5:1-3).

David's master stroke is capturing Jerusalem, a Jebusite city on the border between Judah and Benjamin that belonged to no tribe (2 Sam 5:6-9). It becomes 'the city of David', a neutral capital. He then brings the ark of God there with dancing and sacrifice (2 Sam 6), making Jerusalem the religious as well as political centre. When David wants to build God a house (temple), God turns the idea around: God will build David a 'house', a dynasty, and David's son will build the temple (2 Sam 7:11-13). This promise, the Davidic covenant, becomes one of the pillars of the Old Testament's hope.

The turning point is 2 Sam 11. 'At the time when kings go forth to battle', David stays home, sees Bathsheba bathing, takes her, and when she becomes pregnant arranges the death of her husband Uriah, one of his most loyal soldiers. The prophet Nathan confronts David with a parable about a rich man who steals a poor man's only lamb, and announces that 'the sword shall never depart from thine house' (2 Sam 12:10). The following chapters show exactly that: Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar, Absalom kills Amnon, Absalom revolts and drives David from Jerusalem, and Absalom dies, leaving David weeping, 'O my son Absalom' (2 Sam 18:33).

The book is remarkable among ancient royal writings. Assyrian and Egyptian kings recorded only victories. 2 Samuel records the king's adultery, murder, weakness as a father and failures as a ruler. Many scholars see this as evidence of an authentic prophetic tradition that held kings accountable to God's law.
39940: God promises David a dynasty, a kingdom and a throne forever, with the king treated as God's son. Unlike Sinai, the promise is unconditional in its ultimate outcome, though individual kings can be disciplined.
39942: Ancient kings rewarded loyal servants with land or dynasty grants. Moshe Weinfeld compared God's promise to David to these royal grants.
39944: When Uzzah touches the ark to steady it, he dies. The ark was meant to be carried on poles by Levites, not on a cart like the Philistines did.
39946: Nathan's parable traps David into judging himself. Few ancient courts allowed a prophet to accuse the king to his face.
39948: Taking a king's concubines was a public claim to his throne. Absalom does so on the roof, fulfilling Nathan's words.
39950: In the ancient world a new dynasty often wiped out the old. David instead shows covenant kindness to Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth.
39951:
For Jewish tradition David is the ideal king, the 'sweet psalmist of Israel' (2 Sam 23:1) and the ancestor of the Messiah, often called *Mashiach ben David*. The Davidic covenant of 2 Sam 7 is central to Jewish messianic hope; the blessings recited after the haftarah each Sabbath include a prayer for the return of David's kingdom. The story of David bringing the ark to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:1-7:17) is read as the haftarah alongside the death of Nadab and Abihu (Lev 9-11), pairing two stories of holiness that cannot be handled carelessly. David's song in 2 Sam 22 (almost identical to Ps 18) is the haftarah for the seventh day of Passover, set beside the Song of the Sea.

The rabbis wrestled openly with David's sin. One Talmudic opinion (Shabbat 56a) argues that technically David did not commit adultery, because soldiers gave their wives conditional divorces before battle. But other rabbis insist on the plain sense, and the text itself has God say through Nathan 'thou hast despised the commandment of the LORD' (2 Sam 12:9). The more common rabbinic lesson is that David is the model of the penitent: he admits 'I have sinned against the LORD' (2 Sam 12:13), and Psalm 51 is linked by its heading to this moment. The Talmud says David's repentance was meant to teach that no one is beyond return (Avodah Zarah 4b-5a).

The first audience would have heard 2 Samuel as the story of God's faithfulness to a flawed king. The everlasting promise does not depend on David's goodness, but sin still has terrible consequences inside his family and nation. God remains the true King, the one who 'took thee from the sheepcote' (2 Sam 7:8). David's grateful prayer after the covenant, 'Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that thou hast brought me hitherto?' (2 Sam 7:18), shows the right response: humble wonder at grace.

40005: The Davidic covenant (2 Sam 7:12-16) is one of the main roots of the New Testament's claim that Jesus is the Messiah. Matthew begins 'Jesus Christ, the son of David' (Matt 1:1); Gabriel promises Jesus David's throne (Luke 1:32-33); and Paul says the gospel concerns God's Son 'made of the seed of David according to the flesh' (Rom 1:3). The promise 'I will be his father, and he shall be my son' (2 Sam 7:14) is applied to Jesus in Heb 1:5. The New Testament also draws on the contrasts: David, the king who took another man's wife and life, versus Jesus, the king who lays down his life; David leaving Jerusalem over the Mount of Olives in grief (2 Sam 15:30) has been compared to Jesus' path to Gethsemane. Jewish readers see 2 Sam 7 as the foundation of the hope that a descendant of David will restore Israel in the messianic age; the disagreement with Christians is over whether Jesus is that descendant, not over the importance of the promise.

Nathan's parable casts her as the innocent lamb and David as the thief (2 Sam 12:1-9); God's judgment falls on David. Scholars such as Richard Davidson, Sara Koenig and Robert Alter argue that the narrative treats David's act as abuse of power, some calling it 'power rape'.

40015: Understanding both grace and consequence helps churches respond honestly when leaders fall, caring for victims rather than rushing to restoration.
40016: 2 Samuel grounded Israel's hope in God's unbreakable promise to David's house, while warning kings that God's anointed are not above his law and that sin brings real consequences on families and nations.
